article.overview: A visible-light camera is an imaging instrument that records scene brightness in the part of the spectrum that the human eye can see, commonly taken as wavelengths of about 0.4 to 0.7 micrometres. The class is defined by its spectral band and general imaging purpose rather than by one design. The examples reviewed here are flown: the handheld Hasselblad 500EL cameras used for Apollo lunar-surface photography [1][2], the film-based Lunar Orbiter photographic system of 1966 and 1967 [5], and the ESA SMART-1 Advanced Moon micro-Imager Experiment (AMIE), whose filters extend partly beyond the visible band [8][9]. No prototype or proposed visible-light camera is described, because no authoritative source for one was reviewed for this article.
article.description:
A visible-light camera forms an image from light in the visible band and records it either on photographic film or on an electronic detector such as a charge-coupled device (CCD). The three examples in this article record the band in different ways. The Apollo Hasselblad cameras used film, and NASA's lunar-surface film allowances covered both colour and black-and-white stock [1]. The Lunar Orbiter system was a film-based photographic system with a film processing unit and a readout scanner [5]. The SMART-1 AMIE used a CCD with a set of filters [8][9].

The term describes what the camera is designed to sense. It does not by itself state the detector technology, the field of view, the ground resolution or the mass, which must be taken from the named instrument.

A visible-light camera is distinguished from a panchromatic camera by how the band is defined. A panchromatic camera records one broad band across the visible range in a single channel. A band-defined visible camera can use separate channels, such as colour filters. The ESA mission page describes AMIE as carrying a fixed panchromatic filter together with a three-colour filter set [8], which shows both kinds of channel in one instrument. The sources reviewed do not state the exact passband of AMIE's panchromatic filter, so this distinction is drawn only as far as the sources support.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
Visible-light cameras serve two broad purposes in the sources reviewed. The first is documentation. The Apollo Hasselblad cameras formed the lunar-surface still-photography complement of the Apollo missions. NASA describes the Hasselblad in this role and says a 250 mm telephoto lens was added to that complement for Apollo 15 [2].

The second is orbital imaging of the Moon. The Lunar Orbiter program comprised five uncrewed Moon-orbiting photographic missions launched in 1966 and 1967 [5]. The SMART-1 AMIE was an imaging instrument on a lunar orbiter; ESA describes it as intended to take colour images through three filters at 750, 915 and 960 nm [9].

Terrain mapping, panchromatic mapping and other specialised imaging classes are covered in their own entries. Cross-references: 026 Panoramic camera, 027 High-resolution camera, 043 Panchromatic camera, 044 Wide-angle camera and 045 Narrow-angle camera. The terrain-related lander and orbiter cameras, including the Chang'e-3 topography camera, are discussed in entry 028 Terrain mapping camera. This article does not duplicate those entries.
article.operating_principle:
A lens forms an image of the scene on a detector. In a film camera, the detector is an emulsion whose chemistry changes where light falls, and the exposed film must then be processed and read out. In a CCD camera, light releases electric charge in each pixel, which is read out as a digital signal. The band a camera responds to is set by the detector's sensitivity together with any filter in front of it.

The Lunar Orbiter system carried a film processing unit and a readout scanner as part of its camera assembly [5]. The sources read do not give the processing sequence in detail, so this article does not describe it further.

For AMIE, ESA describes a fixed panchromatic filter together with a three-colour filter set [8] and gives filter wavelengths of 750, 915 and 960 nm [9]. Because the 915 nm and 960 nm filters lie beyond the visible range, the camera's operating band is wider than the visible band alone.
article.scientific_importance:
A visible-light image shows how a surface looks in visible light, which helps observers interpret surface texture, landforms and the layout of equipment. It does not by itself give composition, height or age; those need other measurements or stereo geometry. The photographic record is itself an important product of this class: NASA's astronaut still-photography page describes the Hasselblad as the lunar-surface still-photography complement [2], and NSSDC issued a data users' note on Apollo 11 lunar photography [7]. The frame counts in that note could not be read in this review.

The sources reviewed do not quantify the scientific results obtained from the Lunar Orbiter photographs or from AMIE images, so their scientific importance is described qualitatively here.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a visible-light camera. The three examples differ in platform, detector technology, optics and status, so the values below must not be compared as if they described one product. Each value is tied to the named instrument. Where the sources read do not publish a value, it is reported as not publicly specified.
physical_specifications.comparison_table_markdown:
| Item | Apollo Hasselblad 500EL (lunar surface) | Lunar Orbiter photographic system | SMART-1 AMIE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Status in sources | Flown on Apollo lunar-surface missions [1][2] | Flown; five missions launched 1966 and 1967 [5] | Flown on SMART-1; impact 3 September 2006 [8] |
| Detector | Photographic film, 70 mm, double-perforated magazines [1] | Photographic film; film width conflicts within [5] | CCD; size not stated on the ESA pages reviewed [9] |
| Optics | Data Camera: Zeiss Biogon f/5.6, 60 mm [1]. Other 500EL: Planar f/2.8, 80 mm; Sonnar f/5.6, 250 mm [1] | Medium-resolution: 80 mm, f/2.8 per [5]. High-resolution: 610 mm, f/5.6 per [5] | Focal length and field of view not stated on the ESA pages reviewed [9] |
| Spectral band | Not stated in the sources read [2] | Not stated in the sources read | Filters at 750, 915 and 960 nm, plus a fixed panchromatic filter [8][9] |
| Ground resolution | Not stated in the sources read | Not stated in the sources read | 46 m per pixel at 500 km perilune [9]; 35 m per pixel at 350 km perilune [8] (the two ESA pages differ) |
| Mass, power, dimensions | Not publicly specified | Not publicly specified | Not publicly specified |

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions: not publicly specified in the sources read for the Apollo Hasselblad cameras, the Lunar Orbiter photographic system or the SMART-1 AMIE. No external dimension of any example is given in this article.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass: not publicly specified in the sources read for any of the three examples. Mass affects launch and lander requirements, so this gap matters for any future transport assessment (see the transportation section).
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power: not publicly specified in the sources read for any of the three examples. The sources read do not describe the power budgets of the three examples.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Visible-light cameras must operate in vacuum, with large temperature swings and radiation exposure on the lunar surface or in lunar orbit. The three examples handled these conditions in different ways, and the sources read do not give their thermal, radiation or data-handling requirements in quantitative form.

The Apollo cameras were operated by astronauts on the lunar surface, and their operational constraints were film-related: the ALSJ page gives the number of pictures per film loading [1], and NASA gives film totals per mission [2]. The orbital instruments depend on stable viewing geometry and on power, thermal and data interfaces with their spacecraft; the sources read for AMIE and the Lunar Orbiter system do not specify these interfaces.
article.limitations:
The visible band is only part of the spectrum, so a visible-light camera cannot by itself give composition or temperature. Its images show brightness and colour, not height or chemistry without further measurements.

Film-based systems need processing, scanning or other readout before their images can be analysed. The Lunar Orbiter system carried a film processing unit and a readout scanner for this purpose [5]. The Apollo Hasselblad photography was constrained by the number of frames per film loading [1].

Each example is a different design and mission context. The Apollo cameras were handheld, the Lunar Orbiter system was an orbital film system, and AMIE was a CCD imager with filters. Values should not be transferred between them.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The three examples were delivered in different ways. The Apollo Hasselblad cameras were carried to the lunar surface by the Apollo lunar module and operated by astronauts. The Lunar Orbiter photographic system and the AMIE camera were orbiter payloads. SMART-1 was launched as a secondary payload on Ariane 5 [8]. The sources read do not describe the spacecraft integration interfaces of the Lunar Orbiter or AMIE cameras in enough detail to assess them.
transportation_process: Integrate the handheld camera and its film magazines into the Apollo lunar module for transfer to the surface (Apollo).
Lower the mated magazine and camera from the lunar module to the Commander, who was standing on the surface (Apollo) [1].
Integrate an orbiter camera into the spacecraft payload, with its optics and detector mounted and aligned (Lunar Orbiter, AMIE). The sources read do not specify the mounting or alignment method.
Launch the spacecraft, transfer it to the Moon and insert it into lunar orbit (Lunar Orbiter; SMART-1, per ESA [8]).
Commission the camera in orbit and return its data (AMIE).
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: For the Apollo Hasselblad, deployment was manual: the astronaut carried and operated the camera on the lunar surface [1]. For the Lunar Orbiter photographic system and AMIE, the cameras were fixed payloads of orbiting spacecraft. The sources read do not describe their pointing or mounting mechanisms.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo lunar-surface photography from 1969 onward [1][3]; the Lunar Orbiter missions in 1966 and 1967 [5]; and the SMART-1 AMIE, launched in 2003 and ending with impact in 2006 [8].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted in this article. Any future visible-light camera would need its mass, dimensions, mounting, power, data and thermal interfaces compared with verified vehicle documentation before compatibility could be claimed.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo Hasselblad photographs are a central visual record of the Apollo lunar-surface missions. NASA describes the Hasselblad as the lunar-surface still-photography complement, notes that it was first used on the last two Mercury one-man missions in 1962 and 1963, and says Apollo 8 was the first mission to use the Hasselblad EL electric cameras [2]. The Apollo 11 lunar-surface photographs are dated 20 July 1969 [3]. The Lunar Orbiter program produced photographic orbital missions in 1966 and 1967 [5]. ESA's SMART-1 carried AMIE to the Moon, launched in 2003 and ending with impact in 2006 [8][9].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- **Lunar Orbiter band and document access.** The spectral sensitivity of the film is not stated in the sources read. NASA SP-242 [6] was located, but its scanned PDF had no readable text layer in this review, so its camera-specification pages are unverified.
- **Lunar Orbiter lens and film conflicts.** The Wikipedia summary gives the wide-angle lens as f/2.8 and the film width as both 70 mm and 65 mm Kodak Bimat [5]. A secondary summary gave f/4.5 and is not used. The conflict is unresolved.
- **Apollo frame counts and film types.** The NSSDC Apollo 11 data users' note [7] was located, but its text could not be read in this review; frame counts from search summaries are not used. The sources read do not establish whether the lunar-surface magazines were colour or black-and-white for each set of frames.
- **AMIE band, resolution and in-flight performance.** The ESA pages give filters at 750, 915 and 960 nm and two different resolution figures [8][9]. In-flight image performance was not verified. The detector size and field of view are not stated on the pages reviewed.
- **Images.** The only directly verified image is a Wikimedia Commons file credited to NASA and tagged public domain on Commons [4]. The NASA Apollo images were linked by source page only because their asset URLs did not resolve, and no direct image was verified for the Lunar Orbiter or AMIE examples.
- **Mass, power and dimensions.** These are not publicly specified for any example in the sources read.
- **Cross-references.** Entries 026, 027, 043, 044 and 045 are covered in their own articles, and entry 028 covers terrain and lander topography cameras. This article does not duplicate them.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url, source_page_url and reference URLs in this file have query strings and fragments removed. One image (Wikimedia Commons file) has a verified direct asset and is repeated in the overview and Apollo example arrays. Three NASA image references have image_url null because no direct asset was verified; they carry source-page links, are not rendered as images and are not listed in section arrays. No direct image was verified for the Lunar Orbiter or AMIE examples.

data_quality_notes: Status: Apollo Hasselblad and Lunar Orbiter are flown. AMIE is flown per ESA pages, but its in-flight imaging performance was not verified. No prototype or proposed visible-light camera example was included because no authoritative source for one was reviewed.

Lunar Orbiter: the Wikipedia summary conflicts with itself on film width (70 mm vs 65 mm Kodak Bimat), and the wide-angle f-number is unverified against NASA SP-242, whose scanned PDF could not be read.

AMIE: ESA mission and science pages give different resolution figures (35 m/pixel at 350 km perilune vs 46 m/pixel at 500 km perilune). Both are reported with their sources; field of view and detector size are not stated on the pages read, and the 5.3 degree field of view and 1024 x 1024 CCD from a secondary summary are excluded.
Apollo: the NASA Biogon 5.6/60 mm PDF returned HTTP 404 and is not cited. NSSDC Data Users' Note 70-06 was located but could not be read, so its frame counts are not used.

Images: the only directly verified image is a Wikimedia Commons file (HTTP 200, image/jpeg, public-domain tag from Commons, credit NASA per Commons metadata). It is not an official NASA asset page. NASA image assets named on the ALSJ page returned HTTP 404 at their nasa.gov asset paths, and the NASA image-library asset host returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so they are null with source-page references.
Mass, power and dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources read for any example. No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted.
No lunar landing-site or location recommendation is included, as deferred by the user.
